title: The Riemann Hypothesis, Explained Simply, and Why an AI Just Claimed to Prove It
author: Niaz Bin Siraj
excerpt: On November 20, 2026, an Anthropic mathematician announced that he and the AI model Claude had discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous unsolved problem in all of mathematics. Here is what the hypothesis actually means, why it matters, and why this could change everything.
contents:
On November 20, 2026, a mathematician named Levent Alpoge, who works at Anthropic, posted a quiet but earth-shaking statement on his personal website: "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis." If this claim holds up, it would solve the most famous unsolved problem in all of mathematics, a question that has haunted the brightest minds for 167 years. But what does it actually mean? Let us break it down from the very beginning, in simple words.

What Are Prime Numbers?

Before we can understand the Riemann Hypothesis, we need to understand prime numbers. A prime number is a number greater than 1 that can only be divided evenly by 1 and itself. It has no other divisors.

lightbulb
Think of primes as atoms

Just like every physical object is made of atoms, every whole number is made of prime numbers. The number 12, for example, is 2 x 2 x 3. The number 100 is 2 x 2 x 5 x 5. Primes are the building blocks of all numbers.

Here are the first few prime numbers:

The First 15 Prime Numbers
23571113171923293137414347
Notice the gaps between primes: sometimes they are close (like 2 and 3), sometimes far apart (like 23 and 29). There is no obvious pattern.

At first glance, primes seem completely random. There is no simple formula that tells you "the next prime is here." Sometimes two primes sit right next to each other (like 11 and 13). Other times there is a large gap before the next prime appears. This randomness has puzzled mathematicians for thousands of years.

The Hidden Rhythm of Primes

Here is where it gets interesting. While individual primes appear random, if you zoom out and look at the big picture, something beautiful emerges. Primes become rarer as numbers get bigger, and they thin out in a surprisingly predictable way.

auto_awesome
A simple analogy

Imagine walking through a forest. At first, trees are everywhere, packed close together. As you walk further, the trees start to spread out. You cannot predict exactly where the next tree will be, but you can predict roughly how many trees you will see in every 100 meters. Primes behave the same way along the number line.

Mathematicians discovered a formula called the Prime Number Theorem that tells us, on average, how many primes exist below any given number. For example, below 1,000, there are about 168 primes. Below 1,000,000, there are about 78,498 primes. The formula predicts these counts remarkably well.

25Primes below 10025% are prime
168Primes below 1,00016.8% are prime
78,498Primes below 1,000,0007.8% are prime
50,847,534Primes below 1 billion5.1% are prime

But here is the problem. The formula gives us a smooth average, but the actual count of primes constantly bounces slightly above and below that average. Sometimes there are more primes than expected, sometimes fewer. The big question is: How badly does the actual count deviate from the predicted average? Is the bouncing wild and chaotic, or is it tightly controlled?

This is exactly what the Riemann Hypothesis is about.

The Riemann Zeta Function

In 1859, a brilliant German mathematician named Bernhard Riemann published a short paper, only 8 pages long, that would change mathematics forever. In it, he introduced a special mathematical function called the Riemann Zeta Function.

The Function
Riemann Zeta Function

A mathematical formula that takes a number as input and produces a number as output. It is defined as an infinite sum:

$$\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s} = \frac{1}{1^s} + \frac{1}{2^s} + \frac{1}{3^s} + \frac{1}{4^s} + \cdots$$
The Greek letter zeta (\(\zeta\)) names the function. The input \(s\) can be any complex number. Each term gets smaller as \(n\) grows.

What makes this function so special is a remarkable discovery by Riemann: this function, built from simple fractions of all whole numbers, is secretly and deeply connected to prime numbers. Riemann showed that you can rewrite the same function in a completely different way using only primes. This means that understanding the behavior of the zeta function is the same as understanding the behavior of primes.

$$\zeta(s) = \prod_{p \text{ prime}} \frac{1}{1 - p^{-s}} = \frac{1}{1-2^{-s}} \cdot \frac{1}{1-3^{-s}} \cdot \frac{1}{1-5^{-s}} \cdots$$
The Euler Product: the exact same function, rewritten using only prime numbers. This is the bridge between all numbers and primes.
The Standard Form (Sum)
$$\sum \frac{1}{n^s}$$
Built from every whole number: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ...
The Prime Form (Product)
$$\prod \frac{1}{1-p^{-s}}$$
Can be rewritten using only prime numbers: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ...

This was Riemann's genius. He built a bridge between two worlds: the world of all numbers and the world of primes. If you can understand one side of the bridge, you automatically understand the other.

What Is the Riemann Hypothesis?

Now comes the core question. When mathematicians study functions, they look for the zeros, the specific inputs that make the function output exactly zero. The zeta function has two kinds of zeros:

Trivial Zeros
\(s = -2, -4, -6, \ldots\)
Boring, predictable. We know exactly where they are. They do not tell us anything interesting.
Non-Trivial Zeros
\(\frac{1}{2} + ti\)
Mysterious, important. These hold the secret to understanding prime numbers.

The non-trivial zeros are complex numbers, numbers that have both a "real part" and an "imaginary part." You can think of them as points on a two-dimensional map, where the horizontal axis is the real part and the vertical axis is the imaginary part.

When Riemann plotted where these non-trivial zeros land on the map, he noticed something stunning: they all seemed to line up perfectly on one vertical line. This line sits at the position where the real part equals exactly one-half.

The Hypothesis
The Riemann Hypothesis

All non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have a real part equal to exactly \(\frac{1}{2}\). Formally stated:

$$\text{If } \zeta(s) = 0 \text{ and } s \text{ is non-trivial, then } \operatorname{Re}(s) = \frac{1}{2}$$
Every non-trivial zero \(s\) must lie on the vertical line where the real part equals one-half: the "critical line."
lightbulb
A simple way to picture it

Imagine a straight vertical pole standing in the middle of a field. Now imagine dropping thousands of glowing dots from the sky. The Riemann Hypothesis says that every single dot, without exception, will land exactly on that pole. Not slightly to the left, not slightly to the right, but precisely on the line. Computers have checked over 10 trillion dots, and every single one landed on the pole. But "10 trillion" is not "all" when there are infinitely many dots.

Why Does It Matter Where the Zeros Are?

Remember the question from earlier: how badly does the actual count of primes deviate from the predicted average? The location of these zeros directly controls the answer. If all the zeros sit on the critical line, it means the deviations are as small and well-behaved as mathematically possible. Primes are not chaotic. They follow a deep, hidden harmony.

$$\pi(x) = \operatorname{Li}(x) + O(\sqrt{x} \log x)$$
If RH is true, the prime counting function \(\pi(x)\) (the number of primes up to \(x\)) never strays far from the logarithmic integral \(\operatorname{Li}(x)\). The error term \(O(\sqrt{x} \log x)\) is as tight as the laws of mathematics allow. Primes are as orderly as possible.

If even one zero were off the line, it would mean there are wild, unpredictable swings in where primes appear, regions of numbers with far more or far fewer primes than expected.

167 Years and Counting

The Riemann Hypothesis was proposed in 1859. Since then, it has been one of the most intensely studied problems in the history of mathematics. Some of the greatest mathematical minds of every generation have tried to prove it and failed.

1859
Bernhard Riemann proposes the hypothesis
In an 8-page paper, Riemann connects prime numbers to the zeros of the zeta function and conjectures that all non-trivial zeros lie on the critical line.
1900
Hilbert lists it as a key problem
David Hilbert includes it in his famous list of 23 most important unsolved problems in mathematics. It becomes a central challenge for the 20th century.
1914
Hardy proves infinitely many zeros are on the line
G.H. Hardy shows that infinitely many non-trivial zeros do lie on the critical line, but cannot prove that ALL of them do.
2000
Clay Mathematics Institute offers $1 million
The Riemann Hypothesis is named one of seven Millennium Prize Problems. A correct, peer-reviewed proof earns a one million dollar prize.
2004
10 trillion zeros verified by computer
Computers check over 10 trillion non-trivial zeros. Every single one sits on the critical line. But infinity is bigger than 10 trillion.
Nov 2026
Alpoge and Claude claim a proof
Levent Alpoge of Anthropic releases a massive formal proof written in Lean 4, created in collaboration with the AI model Claude.
167Years UnsolvedSince Riemann's 1859 paper
$1MPrize MoneyMillennium Prize Problem
10T+Zeros VerifiedAll on the critical line
1,000+Theorems at StakeConditional on RH being true

Why It Matters So Much

The Riemann Hypothesis is not just a curiosity for mathematicians. It sits at the foundation of modern number theory, and hundreds of important results across mathematics are built on the assumption that it is true.

1. Thousands of Theorems Depend on It

Over the past century, mathematicians have proven thousands of important results that begin with the words "Assuming the Riemann Hypothesis is true..." These results span number theory, analysis, algebraic geometry, and even physics. If the hypothesis is proven true, all of these conditional results instantly become established mathematical facts.

key
This is like removing scaffolding from a building

Thousands of mathematical "buildings" have been constructed on temporary scaffolding, the assumption that RH is true. Proving RH would replace the scaffolding with a permanent foundation. Everything built on top immediately becomes solid and trustworthy.

2. Understanding the Structure of Numbers

Prime numbers are the atoms of mathematics. Every branch of math that deals with whole numbers eventually touches primes. Proving the Riemann Hypothesis would give us the deepest understanding we have ever had of how these atoms are distributed. It would confirm that there is a beautiful, hidden order beneath the apparent chaos.

3. Connections Across Mathematics and Physics

The Riemann Hypothesis has surprising connections to quantum physics, random matrix theory, and even the spacing of energy levels in atomic nuclei. The zeros of the zeta function behave statistically like eigenvalues of random matrices from quantum mechanics. Proving RH could unlock new understanding at the intersection of pure math and physics.

Fields Connected to the Riemann Hypothesis
Number Theory→Cryptography→Quantum Physics→Random Matrix Theory→Analytic Number Theory
The Riemann Hypothesis sits at the crossroads of multiple major fields. Its proof would send ripples across all of them.

The Announcement: Alpoge and Claude

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic and a junior fellow at Harvard's Society of Fellows, released something the mathematical world had never seen before. Instead of a traditional academic paper, he published a massive formal proof written entirely in Lean 4, a computer proof assistant that verifies mathematical logic step by step.

175,187Source FilesIn the Lean 4 codebase
17MLines of CodeRoughly 17 million lines
239 MBCompressed Size14 archive parts
250,000Pages If PrintedAs traditional text

To put those numbers in perspective: a typical PhD thesis is about 200 pages. A very long mathematics textbook might be 1,000 pages. This proof, if printed, would fill 250,000 pages, roughly the same as 250 full textbooks stacked on top of each other.

warning
No human could read this

A traditional mathematical proof of this size would be impossible for any human to verify. No mathematician could read 250,000 pages and check every logical step. This is precisely why the proof was written in Lean 4, so a computer can verify it instead.

How the Collaboration Worked

Alpoge described an unprecedented division of labor between human and AI:

Alpoge (Human)
Navigator
Steered the research direction, chose the mathematical strategy, translated high-level ideas, and moved frameworks from simple test cases to full generality.
Claude (AI)
Engine
Handled complex technical execution, especially heavy-lifting involving automorphic forms for higher-rank groups, areas outside Alpoge's immediate expertise.

This is a remarkable new model for mathematical research. The human provides the vision and intuition. The AI provides the raw computational and logical power to execute at a scale no human could match.

What Is Lean 4 and Why Does It Matter?

To understand why this proof is different from past claims, you need to understand Lean 4. It is a proof assistant, a computer program that checks mathematical proofs step by step, like a tireless, perfectly logical referee.

Tool
Lean 4 Proof Assistant

A programming language and verification system where every mathematical statement must be justified by explicit logical steps. The computer checks each step against the fundamental rules of logic. If any step is wrong, Lean refuses to accept it.

Traditional mathematical proofs are written in human language, English, with mathematical notation mixed in. They rely on other mathematicians reading them and agreeing that the logic is sound. This works well for short proofs, but it has weaknesses. Humans make mistakes. Humans get tired. Humans can be convinced by arguments that feel right but contain subtle errors.

Lean does not get tired. Lean does not feel. Lean checks every single logical step mechanically. If the proof compiles in Lean, every step follows logically from the ones before it. This is the gold standard of mathematical verification.

Traditional Proof vs Formal Proof
Mathematician Writes Proof→Other Mathematicians Read It→Humans Agree It Is Correct
Traditional approach: relies on human judgment, can miss subtle errors.
Formal Proof Pipeline (What Alpoge Used)
Alpoge + Claude Write Lean Code→Lean Kernel Checks Every Step→Machine Confirms Correctness
Formal approach: every logical step is mechanically verified. No room for hand-waving.

Verification Status: Where Do We Stand?

Within hours of the release, independent mathematicians and computer scientists began auditing the codebase. Here is what they found so far:

Check 1
The code compiles successfully
Independent checks confirmed that all 175,187 source files compile without errors in Lean 4. Every module passes.
Check 2
Lean kernel replay passes
Every module was replayed through Lean's core deduction engine, the most trusted part of the system. All steps verified.
Check 3
Independent kernel checker agrees
An independent Rust-based kernel checker called nanoda also accepted the entire proof structure. This rules out bugs in Lean itself.
Check 4
Axiom audit is clean
MIT's Andrew Sutherland verified that the theorem statements depend only on Lean's standard three foundational axioms. No hidden assumptions, no logical backdoors.
gavel
But verification is not yet complete

While the mechanical checks pass, human mathematicians must still confirm one critical thing: do the formal definitions in the Lean code accurately capture the true meaning of the Riemann Hypothesis? It is possible, in theory, to prove something formally correct in Lean that does not actually mean what you think it means. The mathematical community needs to verify that there are no "semantic loopholes," places where the formal definition subtly differs from the actual mathematical statement.

What Changes If the Proof Is Confirmed?

If this proof survives full scrutiny and is accepted by the mathematical community, the consequences are enormous.

1. Prime Numbers Are Tamed

We would finally have mathematical proof that primes follow a deep, hidden order. The apparent randomness is just surface-level noise. Underneath, there is beautiful structure. The deviations from the average are as small as possible, confirming what mathematicians have suspected for over a century.

2. Thousands of Theorems Become Facts

Every result that starts with "Assuming the Riemann Hypothesis..." instantly drops the assumption. These conditional theorems, spread across number theory, analysis, algebraic geometry, and physics, become unconditional truths. The mathematical landscape solidifies overnight.

auto_awesome
The domino effect

Imagine a room full of dominoes, each one a theorem that depends on RH being true. Proving RH pushes the first domino, and thousands of others fall into place automatically. Entire books of conditional mathematics become unconditional.

3. The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis Too

Alpoge's proof claims to prove not just the standard Riemann Hypothesis, but also the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends the same idea to a broader family of related functions called Dirichlet L-functions. GRH is used even more widely than RH itself, so proving it would have an even larger ripple effect across mathematics.

Wait, Does This Break Internet Encryption?

This is one of the most common questions people ask, so let us address it directly.

key
No, proving the Riemann Hypothesis does not break encryption

Modern encryption like RSA depends on the difficulty of factoring large numbers into their prime components. The Riemann Hypothesis tells us about the overall distribution of primes across the number line, but it does not give you a fast method to factor any specific large number. Knowing the weather pattern across a continent does not tell you if it is raining in your backyard right now.

To be more specific:

  • RSA security depends on the fact that multiplying two huge primes is easy, but reversing that multiplication (factoring) is incredibly hard. RH does not change this.
  • Many algorithms already assume RH is true and work accordingly. If assuming it were enough to break encryption, cryptographers would have noticed long ago.
  • The real threat to RSA comes from quantum computing (specifically Shor's algorithm), not from proving the Riemann Hypothesis.

Your online banking, messaging apps, and passwords are safe from this mathematical breakthrough.

AI as a Mathematician: A New Era

Perhaps the most revolutionary aspect of this announcement is not the mathematics itself, but the method. An AI system did not just assist a human. It performed deep, creative mathematical work at a level that was previously considered uniquely human.

Traditional math proofDozens of pages
Alpoge + Claude proof250,000 pages

No human could have written 17 million lines of formally verified mathematical code alone. The sheer scale of this proof required a new kind of partnership, one where the human provides mathematical vision and the AI provides execution power that would take teams of humans decades to match.

auto_awesome
The pattern is accelerating

In October 2026, OpenAI announced that its AI had disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Now, just weeks later, Anthropic's Claude has helped prove the Riemann Hypothesis. AI is not just assisting mathematicians anymore. It is becoming a mathematician.

What This Means for the Future of Mathematics

If AI can tackle the Riemann Hypothesis, it can likely tackle other unsolved Millennium Prize Problems. There are six remaining:

6Remaining ProblemsMillennium Prize Problems
$1MEach PrizeClay Mathematics Institute
2AI BreakthroughsIn just weeks (Oct-Nov 2026)

The remaining unsolved Millennium Prize Problems include P vs NP, the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, the Yang-Mills existence and mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, and now potentially the Riemann Hypothesis has been crossed off the list.

Key Takeaways

  1. The Riemann Hypothesis is about prime numbers. It says that the apparent randomness of primes hides a deep, beautiful order. All the "zeros" of a special mathematical function line up perfectly on one vertical line.
  2. It has been unsolved for 167 years. Since 1859, the greatest mathematicians in history have tried and failed to prove it. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems with a one million dollar bounty.
  3. An Anthropic mathematician and Claude claim to have proved it. Levent Alpoge released a massive formal proof in Lean 4, containing 175,187 source files and roughly 17 million lines of code, created in collaboration with the AI model Claude.
  4. Machine verification looks promising. The code compiles, passes Lean's kernel checks, passes an independent kernel checker, and depends only on standard foundational axioms. But human review of the semantic correctness is still ongoing.
  5. It does not break encryption. Despite both involving prime numbers, the Riemann Hypothesis and internet security are different problems. Your data is safe.
  6. AI is becoming a mathematician. Two major mathematical breakthroughs in a matter of weeks, both involving AI, suggest we are entering a new era where the boundary between human and machine mathematics is disappearing.

We are watching history unfold in real time. If this proof is confirmed, it will be remembered as one of the greatest intellectual achievements in human history, and also as the moment when AI proved it could stand alongside humans at the highest levels of mathematical thought. The Riemann Hypothesis has waited 167 years for its answer. We may finally have it.
